title: Seeds, batches and variations in video

questions.q: According to the lesson, what is the primary difference between how a seed functions in image generation versus video generation?
options: In images, the seed locks the final pixel values; in video, it only locks the initial noise state.
In images, the seed is ignored; in video, it controls the camera movement.
In images, the seed creates a static latent; in video, the seed creates a temporal loop.
In images, the seed is random; in video, the seed is fixed by the hardware.
questions.answer: In images, the seed locks the final pixel values; in video, it only locks the initial noise state.
questions.why: The lesson states that in image generation, a seed is a 'magic wand' that gives the same picture, but in video, it 'locks the initial state of the noise' while the temporal processing can still introduce variation.

questions.q: Why do consecutive frames in a video latent tensor differ even when the seed is fixed?
options: Because the seed is reset for every frame in the sequence.
Because the frames are statistically independent draws from the noise distribution.
Because the diffusion model intentionally adds random noise to each frame to increase detail.
Because the VRAM runs out and forces a new random seed for subsequent frames.
questions.answer: Because the frames are statistically independent draws from the noise distribution.
questions.why: The lesson explains that 'first_frame (at t=0) and second_frame (at t=1), they are statistically independent draws from the noise distribution,' meaning their values will differ naturally.

questions.q: What is the shape of the latent tensor for video as defined in the 'Under the hood' section?
questions.why: The lesson explicitly states: 'For video, this would typically be (batch_size, channels, time, height, width).'

questions.q: In the context of ComfyUI and video models like SeedVR2, what issue can arise if temporal chunking is not handled with consistent noise seeding or overlapping context?
options: The video will be generated at a lower resolution.
You will see seams or flicker at the chunk boundaries.
The model will crash due to insufficient VRAM.
The audio track will become desynchronized.
questions.answer: You will see seams or flicker at the chunk boundaries.
questions.why: The lesson notes that if chunks are not handled with 'overlapping context or consistent noise seeding across chunks, you will see seams or flicker at the chunk boundaries.'

questions.q: Based on the lab results provided, what does the difference between `first_frame_mean` (0.0859302) and `second_frame_mean` (0.0497632) demonstrate?
options: That the seed failed to lock the noise state.
That the noise is not constant across the temporal dimension.
That the first frame is corrupted by high-frequency artifacts.
That the batch size was too small for accurate sampling.
questions.answer: That the noise is not constant across the temporal dimension.
questions.why: The lesson interprets the lab results by stating: 'This proves that the noise is not constant across time. The variation... is the raw material for temporal flicker if not properly denoised.'
